lens: facts and integrity: every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution in the published JSON checked against the claims ledger, the local ESV copy, the BSB in client/public/bible/ch, the primary texts on disk (APIS translation of P.Oxy. 744, Lake's Didache and Diognetus, ANF Justin and Tertullian, Fyfe's Tacitus, NPNF Augustine Letter 98), and 11 web searches (one WebFetch failed: diotima-doctafemina.org does not resolve in this session)

findings.where: ## What the First Christians Taught, second paragraph (Diognetus): "Then he names what sets them apart, and the first thing he names concerns their children: ..." and "He treats it as one of the few things that would let a neighbor tell a Christian household from any other."
findings.problem: (c) The essay says more than ledger line 22 and the text support. I read Lake's Diognetus today (Perseus XML, scratchpad rome-kids/verify-dl/tlg0646.tlg004.perseus-eng1.xml). At 5.4 the writer already says they "show forth the wonderful and confessedly strange character of the constitution of their own citizenship". At 5.5 he names a distinguishing mark: "They dwell in their own fatherlands, but as if sojourners in them ... Every foreign country is their fatherland, and every fatherland is a foreign country." Both come before 5.6. Ledger line 22 claims only that 5.6 is "the first household practice named", not the first thing named. The second sentence gives the writer a view he never states. He says nothing about what a neighbor could tell, and 5.1 to 5.2 say the distinction between Christians and others is not in customs at all.
findings.fix: Replace "and the first thing he names concerns their children:" with "and the first practice he names concerns their children:". Replace "He treats it as one of the few things that would let a neighbor tell a Christian household from any other." with "It is one of the few marks on his list that a neighbor could actually see." In ledger line 22, quote 5.4 to 5.5 and say that 5.6 is the first practice named.

findings.where: ## Did the Early Christians Rescue Abandoned Babies?, Harris paragraph: "He described it as \"very often but by no means always resulting in death,\" and as a way of moving children who were born free into slavery."
findings.problem: (c) Ledger line 71 records Harris's abstract as saying exposure moved "potential labour out of freedom and into slavery, or at least into de facto slavery". The essay drops that hedge. Because the sentence opens with "He described it as", the paraphrase puts in his mouth a slightly stronger claim than the one he wrote.
findings.fix: "... and as a way of moving children who were born free into slavery, or something close to it."

findings.where: ## The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America, first paragraph: "More than fifteen thousand young people aged out of foster care in 2025 without a permanent family, by the National Council for Adoption's count."
findings.problem: (c) A search today confirms the figure: the NCFA fact sheet Adoption Statistics 2026 (adoptioncouncil.org, as summarized) gives 15,030 for 2025. The same summary says NCFA's foster-care years are federal fiscal years, so these are federal AFCARS numbers that NCFA republishes. Calling it "the National Council for Adoption's count" credits NCFA with the counting. This is a small misattribution, not a wrong number.
findings.fix: "More than fifteen thousand young people aged out of foster care in 2025 without a permanent family, by the federal figures the National Council for Adoption reports." Or keep the sentence and change ledger line 91 to say the figure is FY 2025 AFCARS data as published by NCFA.

findings.where: ## What the Church Did with Foundlings and Their Mothers, Bethany Home paragraph: "Bethany Home in Dublin was run by evangelical Protestants, most of them from the Church of Ireland, the Presbyterians and the Plymouth Brethren."
findings.problem: (f) Ledger line 83 gives the source's order and wording: "in the main, were Plymouth Brethren, Church of Ireland or Presbyterian". It also records that the Church of Ireland says it neither owned nor ran the home. The essay moves the Church of Ireland to the front. That puts the one body that disputes the link first and leans on it harder than the source does.
findings.fix: "Bethany Home in Dublin was run by evangelical Protestants, most of them Plymouth Brethren, members of the Church of Ireland or Presbyterians."

findings.where: Ledger only: correction 9 and line 90 (foster-care count, 30 September 2024)
findings.problem: (c) The ledger contradicts itself. Correction 9 says a search summary reported ACF's FY 2025 report revising the 30 September 2024 count to 327,364. The closing pass on line 90 says no result showed the revised FY 2024 figure. My search today found only the preliminary 328,947 (2024 AFCARS dashboard printable) and no revised number. The essay's "more than 325,000 ... by the federal government's count" holds under either figure.
findings.fix: No change to the essay. In the ledger, mark 327,364 as reported by one search summary that was not seen again, so a later reader does not treat it as confirmed.

clean_checks: Published JSON body (livewell-land/client/public/essays/the-children-rome-threw-away.json) is byte-identical to the body of docs/work/essays/the-children-rome-threw-away.md, which is the text the ledger describes.

Hilarion quotation "if you bear a child and it is male, let it be; if it is female, cast it out." matches the APIS translation word for word (read today in idp.data Translations/20/20442-2.xml, toronto.apis.17). The date (1 BC; "The 29th year of Caesar, Pauni 23") checks out. So do "his sister Alis", staying on in Alexandria, taking care of the child, sending his pay, the Aphrodisias message, "how can I forget you" and "not to worry": all are fair paraphrase. P.Oxy. 744 and Oxyrhynchus are correct.

Didache 2.2, "thou shalt not procure abortion, nor commit infanticide", is verbatim from Lake (Perseus XML read today; a page-break tag falls inside the phrase). The list does begin with murder and adultery.

Diognetus 5.6, "They marry as all men, they bear children, but they do not expose their offspring", is verbatim from Lake. The 5.4 paraphrase (Greek and barbarian cities, local customs in clothing and food) is fair.

Justin, First Apology: "we have been taught that to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men", "almost all so exposed (not only the girls, but also the males) are brought up to prostitution" (ch. XXVII) and "lest some of them be not picked up, but die, and we become murderers" (ch. XXIX) are all verbatim in scripts/data/history-sources/texts/justin-first-apology.html. The "first" reason and the incest paraphrase are accurate, and the citation "27 and 29" is correct.

Tertullian, Apology 9: "with the sin of putting their offspring to death", "by drowning, or by exposure to cold and hunger and dogs" and "murder being once for all forbidden, we may not destroy even the foetus in the womb" are verbatim in tertullian-apology.html. The paraphrase about the crowd and the rulers matches the source, and the charge of killing and eating a child is in ch. 7.

Tacitus, Histories 5.5 (Fyfe, Gutenberg 16927-8.txt lines 11860-11861): "They count it a crime to kill any of their later-born children" is verbatim, with only the capital lowered. "Impious and abominable" a few lines earlier supports "open contempt".

Augustine, Letter 98 (NPNF heading "A.D. 408", to Boniface): "in order to their being cared for by any passer-by" is verbatim. The paraphrase about holy virgins who "neither have nor desire to have children of their own" presenting foundlings for baptism is accurate. The period inside the closing quotation mark is house style, not a change of wording.

Harris quotation "very often but by no means always resulting in death" re-confirmed by search today: the Cambridge Core abstract listing for "Child-Exposure in the Roman Empire", JRS 84 (1994). The page itself was not opened.

Scripture: all 17 passages (Gen 1:27; Mark 10:14, 16; Matt 18:5, 6; Ezek 16:5-6 and 16:6; Exod 1:22; Exod 2:6; Gal 4:5; Ps 68:5-6; Jas 1:27; Matt 2:18; Rom 8:1; Ps 34:18; Ps 27:10; Closing Texts) match the local ESV copy word for word. Each reference matches the verse's sense in the BSB (client/public/bible/ch). LORD is kept as the printed ESV has it. "God sent his Son" (from Gal 4:4) sits outside the quotation marks, and the quoted words are 4:5. Paraphrases of Mark 10:13, Matt 18:2, Exod 2:3-5 and Matt 2:16-17 are faithful.
Mechanics: no em-dashes. The only exclamation points are the two "Live!" quotations, inside verbatim Ezekiel 16:6, each with its reference.

Dates and events: Justin "in the 150s", Tertullian "at Carthage around 197", Constantine's law of 331 (finders keep the child as son or slave), the law under Valentinian I in 374 and the probable ban on exposure the same year, Constantine's conversion about 312 ("nearly a century" before 408), Vaison 442 (re-confirmed by search today; Aleteia: an abandoned child to find sanctuary in a church; the only source is a popular article) and Datheus 787 (archpriest, restored on the closing pass) all agree with the ledger lines.

Historians: Boswell's 20 to 40 percent for urban Romans in the first three centuries, and his view that most abandoned children were rescued, re-confirmed by search today (encyclopedia.com; Goodreads summary). The same summary says infants were left in public places to be found, which supports "often somewhere public where it might be found". Engels (CP 1980) and Harris's reply (CQ 1982), and Stark as a sociologist, are as the ledger says.

Later failures: Kertzer's thesis and "hundreds of thousands" re-confirmed by search today (publisher's description and davidkertzer.com). The Irish commission (January 2021; 18 institutions = 14 + 4; about 56,000 mothers, about 57,000 children, about 9,000 deaths, about 15 percent), Tuam (Bon Secours; Corless; 796; 1925 to 1961), Bethany Home (more than 200 in unmarked graves at Mount Jerome; deaths 1922 to 1949; research 2010) and the Canadian maternity homes all agree with the ledger lines. Fessler's 1945 to 1973 and about 1.5 million re-confirmed by search today (Booklist via icpl.org; Pitt Chronicle).

Post-Christian America: safe haven laws in every state, Texas first in 1999, Baby Moses law. More than 325,000 in foster care on 30 September 2024 (328,947 preliminary, re-seen today). 15,030 aged out in 2025 (NCFA, re-seen today). "Most of those children" matches correction 17. Didache and Tertullian put the unborn and the newborn together ("goes back to them").

Restorations (g): none proposed. Hilarion's original wording ("if it is a male, let it live; if it is a female, expose it."): one search summary today claimed the Diotima page prints it, but WebFetch could not reach diotima-doctafemina.org (host does not resolve in this session) and a second search found no result that uses it. The BMCR review of Bagnall and Cribiore, as summarized, gives a different rendering ("If you bear a child and it is a male, let it live, but if it is female, expose it"). So the writer's wording was not confirmed, and the verified APIS text stays. The "sister ... could mean a wife" clause: a search today again found only the edition's note that brother or sister "often denotes any close relationship", so it is not restored. Foster care "about 329,000 ... preliminary" and aging out "in 2023": not restorable, for the ledger's own reasons. Datheus "archpriest" is already restored.
Ledger status (b): no ledger line the essay relies on is still marked unverified, not checked, open or textbook. The only two open items are original wordings the essay does not use.

Living persons (f): Kertzer ("showed", a published thesis), Corless (found death records for 796 children), Fessler (oral history; women pressured), W. V. Harris ("read the evidence darker", replied to Engels) and Engels (argued a high rate of female infanticide was demographically impossible) are all described fairly and match their published positions. Stark (d. 2022) and Boswell (d. 1994) are not living. The two sentences about Christians on each side of the abortion question are balanced and name no one.

Links: /writing/the-conservative-blind-spot and /writing/the-progressive-blind-spot are status "live" in client/src/lib/shelf.json. /writing/the-early-church-under-rome is "pending" with a rewrite in client/public/essays/, so it is public. The crisis section has the 988 line, the Find Help link, and a plain statement that the essay is not medical or counseling advice.

Small ledger gaps with no essay change needed: "The historian John Boswell" has no line of its own (he was a Yale professor of history, which is textbook). "Americans are deeply divided over what the law should say" and similar framing lines are general and uncontested.
